$comment: The exhibit catalogue, and the only copy of it.
Three programs need to agree about what an exhibit is: the renderer draws it,
the plan validator refuses a script that does not specify one, and the
post-render verifier looks at the pixels to check the drawn thing arrived. Two
of those are Node scripts and one is a Remotion bundle, so the catalogue lives
in JSON that all three import rather than in a TypeScript module one of them
would have to keep a hand-written copy of. A mirrored list is a list that drifts.
`family` decides how honest a kind is allowed to be about numbers:
chart   — its marks encode a measured quantity, so `numeric` fields are
required and the validator refuses prose in them. A bar whose
length came from the frame counter is worse than no bar at all:
it invites the viewer to read a value that does not exist.
diagram — it depicts a mechanism the script already states, and takes its
labels from the script's own lines. Nothing is being measured, so
nothing is being claimed.
Where an exhibit lives in the frame, as a fraction of height.
Every template stacks the same way — hook at the top, exhibit in the middle,
payoff at the bottom — and this is the middle. It is a shared constant
rather than a per-template guess because the verifier samples exactly this
band to decide whether a video showed anything, and a band the layout does
not actually honour would be a check that passes on the wrong pixels.
Top edge clears the tallest three-line hook; bottom edge clears the payoff
block and the safe area platforms overlay their own UI onto.
The order each template reaches for its figures in, most characteristic
first. Both the render-time derivation and the authoring backfill walk
this list, which is why it is here and not in either of them: when it
lived in the TypeScript, the JSON-side tool fell back to plain registry
order and stopped choosing the browser stage for SiteRoast entirely — a
template lost the one figure it was built around, and nothing failed.
First entry is not a default. It is what this template is *for*: a roast
shows the page, a machine joke shows the shell, a recap shows the board.

dial.form: Ring gauge — one ratio against its whole.
dial.why: A single ratio against a limit is a meter, not a chart. The ring is the only figure here that reads at a glance while the number is still counting.

bars.form: Two to four labelled columns, compared against one baseline.
bars.why: Magnitude, low to high. One baseline, one scale — never a second axis.

meters.form: Stacked horizontal meters, one row per item.
meters.why: Long category names, part-to-whole per row. Horizontal because a vertical column cannot carry a label a phone can read.

compare.form: Before against after, as two concentric arcs and the distance between them.
compare.why: The claim of a case study is that something moved. A dumbbell or a nested arc draws the move; two numbers side by side only assert it.

board.form: A four-tile figure board with exactly one tile emphasised.
board.why: A handful of headline numbers is a KPI row, not a grouped bar chart. Emphasis carries the story; the other three tiles are context.

pipeline.form: Stages in sequence with a packet travelling through them.
pipeline.why: Shows where the work goes and where it waits. The packet is the reason it is a video and not a slide.

trace.form: Rows filling in one at a time under a running counter.
trace.why: The cost of a repeated operation is legible only when you watch it repeat. The counter climbing is the whole point.

checklist.form: Steps that run and settle into pass or fail.
checklist.why: A checklist that resolves is a demonstration; a checklist that is merely printed is a caption.

nodegraph.form: A lit core with labelled satellites arriving onto an orbit.
nodegraph.why: For a subject whose shape is one thing feeding many. Arrival order carries the argument.

timeline.form: Editor tracks with clips and a playhead crossing them.
timeline.why: For anything whose subject is sequence or duration. The playhead is a clock the viewer can read without a number.

radar.form: A polar lattice with a sweeping arm and side readouts.
radar.why: For coverage and blind spots — the sweep finds things, which is what a scan is.

cartogram.form: A tile grid map, each region one cell, shaded on one sequential hue.
cartogram.why: A tile grid, not a projection: every region gets equal area and stays legible at phone size, and it never pretends to a geographic precision the script does not have.

code.form: An editor panel typing a snippet, with one line marked.
code.why: For a subject that is literally code. The marked line is the argument; the rest is the context that makes it readable.

browser.form: The page under review, with each fault pinned to the part at fault.
browser.why: The template's original stage. A roast about structure has to show the structure.

terminal.form: A shell that types its command and answers it.
terminal.why: The template's original stage, for the jokes whose setting is a machine.

chat.form: A message thread, arriving one message at a time.
chat.why: The template's original stage, for the jokes whose setting is a person.

sitemock.form: A real page being wrecked round by round.
sitemock.why: LogoLadder and WorksOnMyMachine are built entirely around their own stage and take no other exhibit.
